lead: A short pulse launched into a multimode fiber comes out longer, because its power is shared among many modes and each mode takes a different time to cross the fiber. This is intermodal (or modal) dispersion. It grows with length L and with the fractional index difference Δ, and it caps the bit rate of a multimode link. A graded-index core cuts it by a factor of about 8/Δ, eight hundred times at Δ = 0.01, and a single-mode fiber removes it completely.
prereq: You need: total internal reflection, the critical angle and the fractional index difference Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ from the study of the optical fiber structure.

sections.h3: Step index: two rays, two arrival times

blocks.text: In a step-index fiber the core has one index n₁, so every ray travels at c/n₁ and only the path length differs. The two extremes set the spread. The axial ray goes straight and arrives after t<sub>min</sub> = Ln₁/c. The steepest guided ray meets the core boundary at exactly the critical angle, where sin φ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁; its zig-zag path is L n₁/n₂ long, so it arrives after t<sub>max</sub> = Ln₁²/(cn₂).

blocks.where: δT<sub>s</sub> is the delay difference between the slowest and the fastest ray in s; L is the length in m; n₁ and n₂ are the core and cladding indices; Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁; c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s (3 × 10⁸ is used here).

blocks.text: The approximation drops a factor n₁/n₂ ≈ 1.01. With n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.01, δT<sub>s</sub>/L = 1.48 × 0.01/(3 × 10⁸) = 4.93 × 10⁻¹¹ s/m, that is 49.3 ns per kilometre. The spread grows in proportion to L.

sections.h3: Graded index: fast rays through slow glass

blocks.text: A graded-index core has its highest index on the axis and a smooth fall to n₂ at the core radius a:

n(r) = n₁[1 − 2Δ(r/a)α]1/2 for r < a
n(r) is the index at radius r; a is the core radius; α is the profile parameter (α = 1 triangular, α = 2 parabolic, α → ∞ step).

A ray that swings far from the axis travels a longer path, but most of it lies in lower-index glass where light is faster. With a near-parabolic profile the extra speed almost cancels the extra path, so all rays arrive nearly together. For the near-parabolic profile the delay difference is

blocks.where: δT<sub>g</sub> is the intermodal delay difference of the graded fiber in s; the symbols are as above.

blocks.text: The ratio to the step-index value is Δ/8, so for Δ = 0.01 the 49.3 ns/km of step index falls to 61.7 ps/km. Some books give Ln₁Δ²/(2c) for an exactly parabolic profile analysed by a different ray method; it is of the same order, so quote the form your textbook uses and say which one.

sections.h3: RMS width and the bit-rate limit

blocks.text: A real pulse is not rectangular, so engineers also quote its RMS width σ, the standard deviation of its arrival times. For a rectangular spread of total width δT, σ = δT/(2√3). The two standard results are

blocks.where: σ<sub>s</sub> is the RMS intermodal broadening of a step-index fiber in s.
σ<sub>g</sub> is the RMS broadening of a graded fiber with the optimum profile, α ≈ 2 − 12Δ/5, in s.

blocks.text: The ratio σ<sub>s</sub>/σ<sub>g</sub> is 10/Δ, a thousand at Δ = 0.01. Two bit-rate rules follow, one for each way of measuring the spread:

items: From the full spread: B<sub>T</sub> ≤ 1/(2δT), so that a pulse spreads over at most half of a bit period of a return-to-zero signal.
From the RMS width: B<sub>T</sub>(max) ≈ 0.2/σ, the usual rule for a Gaussian pulse.

blocks.text: Because the spread grows with L, the product of bit rate and length is roughly fixed for a fiber type. This bandwidth–length product is quoted in Mbit/s·km or MHz·km: doubling the reach halves the bit rate. Independent spreads such as intermodal and chromatic dispersion combine as σ = √(σmodal² + σchromatic²). A single-mode fiber guides one mode, so its intermodal term is zero.

examples.question: A multimode fiber has n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01 and length 5 km. (a) Find the intermodal delay difference for a step-index core and the bit-rate limit B<sub>T</sub> ≤ 1/(2δT). (b) Repeat for a near-parabolic graded core.
examples.answer: Step index: 247 ns and about 2 Mbit/s. Graded index: 0.31 ns and about 1.6 Gbit/s, eight hundred times better.

examples.question: For the same fiber (n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01), find the RMS broadening per kilometre and the bandwidth–length product B<sub>T</sub>L from 0.2/σ, for the step-index and the optimum graded profile.
examples.answer: σ = 14.2 ns/km and about 14 Mbit/s·km for step index; σ = 14.2 ps/km and about 14 Gbit/s·km for the optimum graded profile: the factor 10/Δ = 1000.

traps: Using Δ = n₁ − n₂ instead of (n₁ − n₂)/n₁. For n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.465, Δ = 0.0101, not 0.015.
Taking L in km while c is in m/s. Put L in metres, or use the per-kilometre result 49.3 ns/km for n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01.
Mixing the full spread and the RMS width. δT goes with B ≤ 1/(2δT); σ goes with B ≈ 0.2/σ. A rectangular spread has σ = δT/(2√3).
Writing the graded improvement as Δ. It is Δ/8 for the full spread and Δ/10 for the RMS width of the optimum profile.
Expecting intermodal dispersion in a single-mode fiber. With one mode there is no modal delay; its spread is chromatic or polarization mode dispersion.

quiz.q: Define intermodal dispersion and say in which fibers it occurs.
quiz.a: Pulse spreading because different guided modes take different times to cross the fiber. It occurs only in multimode fiber.

quiz.q: Why does a graded-index profile reduce intermodal dispersion?
quiz.a: Rays far from the axis travel longer paths, but in lower-index glass where they are faster; with a near-parabolic profile the extra speed almost cancels the extra path.

quiz.q: A step-index fiber has n₁ = 1.5, Δ = 0.02 and L = 2 km. Find δT and the bit-rate limit B ≤ 1/(2δT).
Repeat the previous question for a near-parabolic graded fiber with the same n₁, Δ and L.
Find the RMS broadening per km of a step-index fiber with n₁ = 1.46 and Δ = 0.015.
A 3 km multimode link must carry 100 Mbit/s with B ≤ 1/(2δT). With n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.01, which core profile works?
quiz.a: Allowed δT = 1/(2 × 10⁸) = 5 ns. Step index gives 49.3 × 3 = 148 ns: fails. Near-parabolic graded gives 61.7 ps × 3 = 0.185 ns: passes, so only the graded fiber works.

quiz.q: Why is the bandwidth–length product used to rate a multimode fiber instead of a plain bandwidth?
quiz.a: The intermodal spread grows in proportion to L, so the bit rate falls as 1/L; the product B<sub>T</sub>L stays roughly fixed and describes the fiber at any length.

beyond: Data-centre multimode fiber is graded-index and rated by its effective modal bandwidth at 850 nm: the OM3, OM4 and OM5 grades reach 2000 to 4700 MHz·km and carry 10 to 100 Gbit/s over a few hundred metres from VCSEL sources. Over long multimode links mode coupling makes the spread grow more slowly than L. Few-mode fibers for space-division multiplexing treat each mode as its own channel and separate them with MIMO processing. Search for “effective modal bandwidth OM4” and “few-mode fiber MIMO”.

figure.caption: In the step-index core (top) the steepest ray zig-zags at the critical angle and over 5 km falls 247 ns behind the axial ray. In the graded core (bottom) the off-axis ray curves back smoothly through faster, lower-index glass and falls behind by only 0.31 ns.

spec.aria: Two fiber cores 5 kilometres long. Top: a step-index core with a straight axial ray and a zig-zag ray, 247 nanoseconds apart at the end. Bottom: a graded core with a straight axial ray and a smoothly curving ray, 0.31 nanoseconds apart.
